response.text:
Recent evidence supports perturbation probes, but does not establish HSTU-specific intent diagnostics. [HSTU (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) models high-cardinality, nonstationary interaction streams; its architecture alone does not demonstrate dependence on recent intent. [Does It Look Sequential? (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) compares original and shuffled sequences across 15 datasets, finding weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. [Disentangling User and Item Sequence Patterns (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) distinguishes user behavior from item-availability effects using random versus constrained shuffling. Order sensitivity can therefore reflect multiple temporal signals.

[Betello et al. (ECIR 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13165) found that removing recent interactions harmed the studied sequential recommenders more than removing beginning or middle interactions; they also introduced Finite Rank-Biased Overlap for comparing finite recommendation lists. These training-data perturbation findings motivate, but do not validate, frozen-HSTU inference probes. Practical adaptation: use training-history next-item examples with fixed targets and candidates; compare intact histories, recent-window retention/old-prefix removal, recent-suffix removal, and shuffling with the last item fixed or shuffled. Preserve left padding and read the final nonpadding position. Report paired target-rank and reciprocal-rank changes, top-10 overlap, and results by history length; calibrate deletion effects against equal-size random deletions and repeat random permutations. Bootstrap paired differences by user. Recent-window retention and old-prefix removal are equivalent when their cutoffs match. Interpret results as model dependence on available sequence information, without claiming causal user intent; keep the host evaluator unchanged.
